strengths: Addresses a clearly important and practically relevant problem: mode collapse/lack of diversity for tail classes in class-conditional diffusion models trained on long-tailed data.

The core idea is well motivated both empirically (Fig. 4/7/10/11 show low-frequency similarity between conditional/unconditional denoising at large t, and mode collapse for tail classes) and theoretically (the mutual-information decomposition in Eq. 2 gives a clear, convincing argument for why naively applying contrastive loss directly on conditional latents admits a degenerate shortcut solution, motivating the proposed indirect diversification via unconditional latents + alignment).

Very thorough experimental validation: results are reported across five datasets (ImageNet-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT), at multiple training checkpoints/imbalance factors, and on both UNet/DDPM and DiT/SiT backbones, showing consistent improvements in FID, FID_tail, IS, sFID, precision/recall, and KID over strong recent baselines (CBDM, REPA, Dispersive Loss, OCLT, DiffROP, UTLO-inspired GAN alignment).

Extensive ablations (loss weight search, batch-resampling interaction, choice of latent encoder depth, alignment-loss time scheduler) support the design choices and show the two losses are complementary/synergistic rather than redundant.

Good qualitative and interpretability analyses beyond FID numbers: t-SNE/density visualizations of tail-class sample distributions, nearest-neighbor analysis exposing literal memorization/mode collapse in the baseline, and frequency decomposition of the reverse process supporting the alignment-loss motivation.

Practical considerations are addressed, including an implementation trick to reduce the ~2x forward-pass overhead to ~1.3x slowdown, and a fair 700k-vs-900k step comparison confirming gains aren't just from extra compute.
Clear attribution/discussion of relationship to concurrent and prior works (Dispersive Loss, CBDM, REPA, UTLO), with explicit discussion of what differs conceptually.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is an incremental but reasonable combination of existing components (InfoNCE-style unsupervised contrastive loss, distillation/alignment loss between conditional and unconditional predictions); novelty lies more in the specific application and combination than in a fundamentally new mechanism.

Diversity claims are argued indirectly via FID/Recall and qualitative visualizations rather than a direct intra-class diversity metric (e.g., pairwise LPIPS within a class), which would more directly substantiate the central diversity claim.

Recall sometimes decreases for CCUA relative to baselines at later training steps (e.g., Table 1 at 900k: CCUA recall 17.3 vs. SiT 18.6, REPA 19.8), which is not discussed despite recall being one of the two headline metrics ("quality and diversity") emphasized in the paper.

The mutual-information argument (Eq. 2) is intuitive but not rigorously formalized (no proof that the trivial/shortcut solution is actually reached in practice for the conditional contrastive baseline, only cited from concurrent work); a more rigorous or empirical direct validation of the claimed shortcut would strengthen the theoretical narrative.

Hyperparameter ablation in Table 5 shows fairly inconsistent trends across (α, γ) combinations (e.g., precision/recall trade-offs move non-monotonically), suggesting some sensitivity to tuning that is not deeply analyzed.

Experiments are capped at 256×256 resolution and up to 900k steps; it remains unclear how benefits scale to larger, longer-trained, or higher-resolution generative pipelines more representative of current large-scale practice.

Minor clarity issues: notation-heavy derivation in Sec. 3.2/3.3 could better foreground intuition before equations, and some inconsistencies in table color-coding descriptions/labels across the appendix reduce readability.
